question_text: A photon and an electron have equal energy $E$. The ratio $\frac{\lambda_{\text{photon}}}{\lambda_{\text{electron}}}$ is proportional to
solution: For a photon, $E = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{\text{photon}}} \implies \lambda_{\text{photon}} = \frac{hc}{E}$. For an electron, the de Broglie wavelength is $\lambda_{\text{electron}} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mE}}$. Thus, $\frac{\lambda_{\text{photon}}}{\lambda_{\text{electron}}} = \frac{hc/E}{h/\sqrt{2mE}} = c\sqrt{\frac{2m}{E}} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{E}}$.

question_text: The cut off wavelength for a metal is $5000\text{ \AA}$. When light of wavelength $3000\text{ \AA}$ falls on it, the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected photoelectron is $E$. When light of wavelength $2000\text{ \AA}$ falls on it, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons will be
solution: From Einstein's photoelectric equation, $K_{\text{max}} = hc\left(\frac{1}{\lambda} - \frac{1}{\lambda_0}\right)$. In the first case, $E = hc\left(\frac{1}{3000} - \frac{1}{5000}\right) = \frac{2hc}{15000} = \frac{hc}{7500}$. In the second case, $E' = hc\left(\frac{1}{2000} - \frac{1}{5000}\right) = \frac{3hc}{10000}$. Taking the ratio, $\frac{E'}{E} = \frac{3/10000}{1/7500} = 2.25$, so $E' = 2.25E$.

question_text: Monochromatic light of wavelength $3000\text{ \AA}$ is emitted from a point source and falls on a photoelectric cell perpendicular to its surface $0.75\text{ metres}$ away from the source. The photocurrent is stopped by applying a suitable negative potential to the anode with respect to the cathode. The point source is now moved to a distance of $1.5\text{ m}$ from the photoelectric cell (light from source continues to fall on the photoelectric cell perpendicular to its surface). Then
options: The photocurrent will be stopped again by the same stopping potential applied earlier
If the stopping potential is made to be $0$ in both cases (before and after displacing the point source) the photocurrent is halved
The photocurrent will be stopped again by half the stopping potential applied earlier
If the stopping potential is made to be $0$ in both cases (before and after displacing the point source) the photocurrent remains the same
solution: Stopping potential depends solely on the frequency (or wavelength) of the incident radiation and the work function of the cathode material ($eV_0 = \frac{hc}{\lambda} - \phi$). Since the wavelength remains $3000\text{ \AA}$, the stopping potential remains completely unchanged.

question_text: The ratio of kinetic energy of an electron and the energy of a photon, both having the same wavelength is
options: Proportional to the wavelength of the photon
Proportional to the energy of the photon
Proportional to the kinetic energy of the electron
Proportional to the magnitude of velocity of the electron
solution: For an electron of velocity $v$, its momentum is $p = mv = \frac{h}{\lambda}$, so its kinetic energy is $K_e = \frac{p^2}{2m} = \frac{pv}{2} = \frac{hv}{2\lambda}$. The energy of the photon of wavelength $\lambda$ is $E_p = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$. The ratio is $\frac{K_e}{E_p} = \frac{hv/(2\lambda)}{hc/\lambda} = \frac{v}{2c}$, which is directly proportional to the magnitude of the velocity of the electron.

question_text: Maximum kinetic energy of a photoelectron is $E$ when the wavelength of incident light is $\lambda$. The energy becomes four times when wavelength is reduced to one third, then work function of the metal is
solution: Given $E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} - \phi \implies \frac{hc}{\lambda} = E + \phi$. When the wavelength is reduced to $\lambda/3$, the maximum kinetic energy becomes $4E$: $4E = \frac{hc}{\lambda/3} - \phi = 3\left(\frac{hc}{\lambda}\right) - \phi = 3(E + \phi) - \phi = 3E + 2\phi$. This gives $E = 2\phi$. Substituting into the first equation: $\frac{hc}{\lambda} = 2\phi + \phi = 3\phi \implies \phi = \frac{hc}{3\lambda}$.
